newsitem.title: ISRAEL: Israel's Treasury seeks to encourage savings.
newsitem.headline: Israel's Treasury seeks to encourage savings.

text.p: Finance Minister Yaacov Neeman on Tuesday told parliament's finance committee that among the proposals he intends to submit to the Israeli cabinet will be a plan to encourage long-term savings.

Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu has asked the Treasury to present to the cabinet on August 10 proposals for structural reforms aimed at stimulating growth. The Treasury will submit these along with its 1998 economic forecast.

Last year it proposed a package of reforms aimed at stimulating investment in the capital markets and encouraging long-term savings. The package was shelved because a key recommendation -- taxing short-term savings -- was deemed too controversial.
"We want to encourage long-term savings," Neeman told the committee.
He said the Treasury was also considering introducing measures in next year's budget to increase investment in infrastructure, creating jobs over the long term.
Unemployment is on the rise as the Israeli economy slows.

Neeman said proceeds from privatisation must go to "creating benefits to the economy" and to lowering debt. He would not expand on this but said only that it was a mistake to use money from privatisation to raise government expenditures.
Tax reform is another Treasury priority, Neeman said. He said he was working with the state revenue administration to bring proposals for 1998 that will lower the tax burden but widen the tax base.
"Foreign investment will become a main source of funding in Israel in the future," he added.
Neeman also said he favoured the independence of the central Bank of Israel but said the system must be "balanced".
The central bank, which alone sets interest rates, has clashed in the past with the Treasury, which has urged an easing of monetary policy. -- Jerusalem newsroom, 972-2-537-0502
